Metadata.title: Localify - Local domains and trusted HTTPS for developers
Metadata.description: Localify is a free, open source app that gives local projects stable .localify domains, trusted HTTPS, DNS routing, and a native macOS control app, without mkcert, /etc/hosts edits, or tunnel setup.

Hero.description: Name your projects instead of juggling ports. .localify URLs, local DNS, trusted HTTPS.
Hero.availability: Free and open source under the AGPL. Desktop app for macOS.

DemoDialog.title: Want to try Localify for real?
DemoDialog.description: Download the desktop app and set up your first local domain.

Agents.title: Let your agent handle everything.
Agents.description: Connect Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor to Localify. Your agent sets up the project, runs your services, and cleans up its worktrees when it's done. You just talk to it.

urls.title: URLs that mean something.
urls.body: studio.localify, admin.localify, docs.localify. No more juggling :3000, :3001, :5173.

ui.title: An app, not a CLI.
ui.body: Your projects, their URLs, their logs — all in one place. No config files to edit.

agents.title: Many agents, zero conflicts.
agents.body: Cursor, Claude Code and your own dev servers running side by side. Each project keeps its stable URL.

HowItWorks.description: One permission at install. A folder or a localify init-project. One domain per app, in HTTPS. That's it.

steps.title: One password, zero config.
steps.body: On first launch, Localify asks for your administrator password once. Then it sets up the certificate authority, DNS, and the daemon by itself. The first time you need HTTPS in a browser, macOS asks you to confirm the certificate once.

steps.title: Pick a folder. Localify autocompletes.
steps.body: Localify scans the folder, detects its apps, and suggests a hostname for each. You review and confirm.

steps.title: localify init-project, straight from your editor.
steps.body: Already in your editor? Run localify init-project from the terminal. Same autocomplete flow, same confirmation. The project shows up in the app.

steps.title: Projects by name, not by port.
steps.body: Every project has its .localify hostnames with trusted HTTPS. Tabs that mean something, demos that look like the product, envs that stop breaking when a port changes.

steps.title: Launch, monitor, no editor needed.
steps.body: Localify doubles as your local dashboard: one click to start any project, one glance to see what's running. Perfect for vibecoding without ever opening your IDE.

Faq.description: The short answers. If we missed one, drop us a line.

items.question: What is Localify?
items.answer: Localify gives every local project a stable .localify URL with trusted HTTPS. Instead of juggling localhost:3000, localhost:5173, and localhost:8080, you open app.localify or admin.localify directly in your browser.

items.question: Is it free?
items.answer: Yes. Localify is free and open source under the AGPL, with no account and no limit on projects or domains. The source code is on GitHub. Public URLs are the one paid part: they run on Localify Cloud and need a Pro plan, which starts with a 7-day free trial.

items.question: Who is it for?
items.answer: For developers running multiple apps locally, switching between stacks, or letting AI agents work in parallel — without managing port conflicts.

items.question: Does it put my work online?
items.answer: Only if you ask. Your local services stay on your machine, and no app traffic or request log is sent to Localify. The exception is a public URL, a paid option you turn on for one domain at a time: requests to that URL go through Cloudflare to your machine, behind a password by default.

items.question: Does Localify collect analytics?
items.answer: The official desktop app does: product flows (onboarding, navigation, project creation), usage counts, and error reports. These events don't include request logs, project names, domains, local paths, or traffic content. A filter removes URLs, file paths, .localify domains, and quoted names from error reports before they're sent, though it can't catch everything. The CLI and daemon send no analytics.

items.question: Which platforms does it run on?
items.answer: The desktop app runs on macOS on Apple Silicon for now. The CLI and daemon also install on Linux x86_64 with curl -fsSL https://localify.dev/install.sh | sh, and build from source elsewhere. Windows and a Linux desktop app are planned for later.

items.question: Do I need to edit /etc/hosts or install mkcert?
items.answer: No. Localify handles the local resolver, local certificate authority, and Node trust setup during onboarding. After that, new .localify hostnames work without per-project setup.

items.question: Does it work with Docker, Next.js, or my framework?
items.answer: Yes. Localify routes by hostname, so anything that listens on a local port works. Docker, Next.js, Vite, Rails, your own server — whatever your stack.

items.question: How is it different from ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel?
items.answer: ngrok and Cloudflare Tunnel are built to put services on the internet. Localify is built for local development: clean URLs and trusted HTTPS on your machine, with no cloud. When you need to open a dev server from your phone or another computer, a public URL does it, behind a password by default. Public URLs come with Localify Cloud Pro.

items.question: Does it work with Cursor, Claude Code, or multiple AI agents in parallel?
items.answer: Yes — it's actually a core use case. Run /localify in any project and your agent sets everything up: a domain per app, trusted HTTPS, and dev scripts. Multiple agents can then work on different apps in parallel without any port conflicts.

items.question: What stays free?

items.question: How does the trial work?

items.question: What counts as a serving machine?
items.answer: A computer that puts your public URLs online through Localify Cloud. Pro lets 2 do it at the same time, for example your laptop and the machine your agents run on. Signing in on another computer doesn't use one.

items.question: Can I cancel or get a refund?
items.answer: Cancel any time from the customer portal. Pro stays on until the end of the period you paid for, then stops: your public URLs stop serving but are kept, with their addresses and passwords. For your first charge, write to support@localify.dev within 14 days for a full refund.

items.question: Who handles the payment?
items.answer: Polar (polar.sh), as merchant of record. Polar is the seller, takes the payment, handles sales tax and VAT, and sends your invoices. Your card details go to Polar and its payment processor, never to us.

items.question: What can I use public URLs for?
items.answer: Reaching your own dev servers from a phone or another computer, and showing work in progress. Not production hosting: each account has a request limit for bursts of traffic. Phishing, malware, illegal content, and infringement are forbidden and get the URL taken down.

Terms.title: Terms of Service
Terms.intro: Localify is free and open source, and its license covers most of how you can use it. These terms add the rest: the paid Localify Cloud service behind public URLs, and the website. If anything is unclear, write to support@localify.dev.

sections.title: 1. Who we are
body: Localify is made by Téo Goulois ("we"). It is a local development proxy: a Rust daemon, a CLI, and a desktop app that route .localify domains to services on your own machine with trusted HTTPS.

sections.title: 2. The software license
body: The Localify software is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 only (AGPL-3.0-only). That license governs how you can use, modify, and redistribute the software. Nothing on this page takes away a right it gives you.

sections.title: 3. What's free and what's paid
body: The Localify software is free: no purchase, no license key, no activation limit, and no account. Public URLs are the exception. They run on Localify Cloud, a paid service with its own account, described in section 6.

sections.title: 4. Name, logo, and media
body: The AGPL doesn't cover the Localify name and logo, and they aren't licensed to you. If you distribute a modified version, give it your own name and logo. The images and videos on this website and in the app aren't licensed under the AGPL either.

sections.title: 5. No warranty
body: Localify is provided "as is", with no warranty of any kind, to the extent the law allows. Sections 15 and 16 of the license set out the disclaimer of warranty and the limitation of liability. Localify is a developer tool. It isn't meant for production traffic, public hosting, or as a security boundary for untrusted services.

sections.title: 6. Localify Cloud
body: Public URLs, at https://<slug>.localify.fyi and served from your machine, run on Localify Cloud. You sign in with GitHub, and serving a public URL needs a paid plan. Localify Cloud Pro costs $7.99 a month or $79 a year, in US dollars, and includes 2 machines serving public URLs at the same time and 10 public URLs.

Polar (polar.sh) sells the plan as merchant of record. Polar is the seller of record: it takes the payment, handles sales tax and VAT, and issues your invoices. Polar's checkout buyer terms also apply to the payment.

We can change Localify Cloud or stop it. We tell subscribers at least 30 days before a material change. If we stop it, each subscriber gets a pro-rata refund of the prepaid time they haven't used. There is no uptime commitment or service level agreement, and Localify Cloud may be unavailable at times. This doesn't limit the legal guarantee of conformity you have as a consumer.

sections.title: 6.1 Trial, renewal, and cancellation
body: Pro starts with a 7-day free trial. Checkout asks for a card, and nothing is charged until the trial ends. If you cancel before then, you pay nothing. There is one trial per GitHub account.

After the trial, the plan renews automatically every month or every year, as you chose, and Polar charges your card at each renewal until you cancel. In Polar's customer portal, which you open from the app or with localify billing, you can cancel, switch between monthly and yearly, and update your card at any time.
When you cancel, the plan doesn't renew, and you keep Pro until the end of the period you've already paid for.

When Pro ends, your public URLs stop serving, but they're kept, with their addresses and passwords, and serve again if you subscribe again. Your account and your sign-in stay too. Deleting a URL or the account is a separate step: remove a URL from the app or with localify public-url remove, and write to support@localify.dev to delete the account.

sections.title: 6.2 Refunds
body: For your first charge, write to support@localify.dev within 14 days of it and we'll refund it in full, whatever the reason. Other charges for a period that has started aren't refunded, except as section 6 or the law provides.

If you're a consumer in the European Union, France included, you also have a legal right to withdraw from the subscription within 14 days of subscribing, without giving a reason. If you asked for the service to start during those 14 days, as a trial does, withdrawing means paying for the service provided until then, pro rata. Nothing is charged during the free trial, so withdrawing during it costs nothing.
To withdraw, tell us before the 14 days are over, by email to support@localify.dev. You can use this model form, but you don't have to. We handle the withdrawal with Polar.
quote: I hereby give notice that I withdraw from my contract for the provision of the following service: Localify Cloud Pro.
GitHub account and checkout email: [username, email]

sections.title: 6.3 Acceptable use
body: Public URLs are for reaching your own dev servers and showing work in progress. They aren't for production hosting or for serving a site to the public. Each account has a request limit that absorbs bursts, such as a page loading hundreds of files at once. Requests above it are refused for a short while.
Don't use a public URL for phishing, malware, illegal content, or content that infringes someone else's rights. You're responsible for what your public URLs serve.

If a public URL breaks these rules, we take it down. After a serious breach, we can also close the account, and the current period isn't refunded, to the extent the law allows. To report abuse, write to abuse@localify.dev.

sections.title: 7. Using the website
body: These terms also cover the website, localify.dev. Don't use it for anything illegal, and don't try to break it, overload it, or get into parts of it that aren't public.

sections.title: 8. Changes to these terms

Privacy.title: Privacy Policy
Privacy.intro: Your local development environment stays on your machine. The desktop app and CLI keep DNS, TLS, routing, projects, and request logs there. This page covers the cases where data does leave your device, and what the website collects.

sections.title: 1. The short version
body: Localify doesn't keep request logs or anything about the traffic of the services you run. Requests to a public URL pass through Cloudflare and Localify Cloud on their way to your machine, without being stored. Localify's analytics leave out local paths, and a filter removes them from error reports. The proxy works locally after setup. Data reaches us in six cases: you visit the website, the official desktop app sends product analytics and error reports, the app checks for updates, you sign in to Localify Cloud and use public URLs, you pay for a Localify Cloud plan through Polar, or you email us.

sections.title: 2. Who we are
body: Téo Goulois ("we") is the data controller for the data described on this page. You can reach us at support@localify.dev.

sections.title: 3. The desktop app and CLI
body: The Localify daemon, desktop app, and CLI run on your machine. DNS, TLS certificates, routing, project configuration, and request logs are handled there. Our analytics don't include the hostnames you create, and the filter described below removes .localify domains from error reports. The requests you proxy on your machine and the logs shown in the app stay there. Public URLs are covered in the next section. The CLI and the daemon send no analytics.

Official desktop builds send product analytics to PostHog: screens viewed, onboarding steps, actions such as creating a project or adding a domain, and counts such as how many projects and domains you have. These events don't include project names, domains, local paths, proxied URLs, or traffic. Autocapture is off. A build made from source without a PostHog token sends nothing.

The app also reports errors to PostHog: the error's name and message, plus hashes that group identical errors. Before sending, a filter removes URLs, file paths, .localify domains, and quoted names. It matches patterns, so it can miss something in an unusual message.
Session replay is off by default and only starts if you turn it on in the app's settings. Replay masks text and inputs, and it doesn't record console logs or network timing.

When the packaged app starts, it checks for updates by fetching release metadata from our download host. That request can leave standard server logs: IP address, user agent, time, and requested file. We use them to deliver updates and troubleshoot delivery, not to build a usage profile.

sections.title: 4. Localify Cloud and public URLs
body: Public URLs are optional and need a paid plan. They need a Localify Cloud account, which you create by signing in with GitHub. We keep your GitHub account's numeric ID and username for as long as the account exists, to recognize you when you sign in. For each computer you sign in from, we keep its name, the local port its tunnel connects to, and a sign-in token stored only as a hash. We never see your GitHub password, and the GitHub token used during sign-in is used once to read your username, then discarded. A signed-in computer asks Localify Cloud every 5 minutes which public URLs it serves; its requests include its Localify version.

For each public URL, we keep its address, the local domain it opens (such as web.journal.localify), the computer that serves it, its settings, and, when it's protected, a salted hash of its password. The password passes through Localify Cloud when you set it but is never stored. We also keep technical identifiers, statuses and dates. A removed URL is kept for 30 days, so its address can't serve someone else's page, then deleted by the next hourly cleanup. Until then, you can take the address back.

Requests to a public URL go through Cloudflare, which runs Localify Cloud, then through a Cloudflare Tunnel to your computer. Localify Cloud checks access and passes each request on, with the visitor's IP address, without logging or storing it. To slow down password guessing and sign-in abuse, Cloudflare limits password attempts per URL and IP address, and sign-in requests per IP address, over one-minute windows. A protected URL sets one cookie on its own address, valid for 7 days, which only records that you entered the password. Localify Cloud logs its errors, not each request. An error message can include details of the request that caused it, and Cloudflare keeps these logs for up to 7 days.

sections.title: 5. Paying for Localify Cloud
body: Plans are sold by Polar (polar.sh), the merchant of record. When you start a trial or subscribe, Polar and its payment processor receive and process your name, your email address, your payment details, and the billing address or country that taxes depend on. Your card details never reach us. Polar sends your receipts and invoices, and its own privacy policy covers what it does with this data.

From Polar, Localify Cloud keeps only your Polar customer ID, your subscription IDs, and your plan's status, such as trial, active, or canceled, with the date its trial or current period ends, plus whether your account has used its one trial. Polar tells us when a subscription changes, and we ask it for your subscriptions to keep that status current.

sections.title: 6. Older versions of the app
body: Older versions of the app used license keys. If you activated a key on one of them, that version may still contact licences.localify.dev to validate it, sending the key and a machine fingerprint. The fingerprint is a non-reversible identifier derived from a stable machine identifier. The current version has no license check and doesn't make this request.

Keygen, the licensing provider, holds the records of those activations, including the platform, hostname, and device name sent at activation when available. They stay there until deleted on request. To ask for deletion, email support@localify.dev.

sections.title: 7. The website
body: In production the website uses two analytics tools, Umami and PostHog. They record page views and clicks on buttons such as download. We don't run advertising trackers or cross-site retargeting.
Umami runs for every visitor. It's loaded from analytics.teogoulois.com and uses no cookies.

PostHog runs only if you accept in the cookie banner. It then keeps a visitor identifier in a cookie and in local storage, and records that you accepted. Its autocapture and session recording are off. If you decline, PostHog sends and stores nothing. If you accepted and change your mind, it stops recording and clears what it stored in your browser. Either way, a local storage entry remembers your choice, and you can change it from the Cookies link in the footer.

If you accepted, clicking a download button may copy a short Localify attribution token to your clipboard, replacing what was there. If you didn't, the website leaves your clipboard alone. When the desktop app starts, it reads the clipboard and ignores anything that isn't such a token. If it finds one, it links your website visit to the app in our analytics. The token contains a PostHog visitor identifier, an attribution ID, a source label, and a timestamp. It doesn't contain project data, domains, local paths, or traffic.

sections.title: 8. Service providers
body: We use these providers:

list.name: Cloudflare
list.description: hosting for the website, the downloads, the update files, and Localify Cloud, including the requests to public URLs.

list.name: Polar
list.description: checkout, payments, sales tax, and invoices for Localify Cloud plans, as merchant of record, with its payment processor.

list.name: PostHog
list.description: website analytics if you accept, plus product analytics and error reports from the desktop app.

sections.title: 9. Why we process this data
body: We rely on your consent for PostHog on the website, and you can withdraw it at any time from the Cookies link in the footer. We process Umami analytics, desktop app analytics, and error reports because we have a legitimate interest in understanding how Localify is used and fixing what breaks. We process update requests to deliver updates, Localify Cloud data to provide the public URLs you signed in for, and support emails to answer you.
We process billing data from Polar to provide the plan you pay for.

sections.title: 10. Retention
body: We keep support emails for as long as they're useful for support, then delete them. PostHog keeps analytics events for up to 7 years, the period set by our plan, which we can't shorten, and session recordings, if you turn them on, for up to 3 months. Umami data is kept for as long as the project runs, unless we delete it sooner. Localify Cloud keeps your account and computers until you ask us to delete them, and removed public URLs for 30 days. Server logs stay with the providers above, under the retention settings of each service. Existing license records stay with the provider until deleted on request.
Localify Cloud keeps your Polar IDs and plan status for as long as your account exists. Polar keeps payment and invoice records under its own policy and for as long as tax law requires.

sections.title: 11. Your rights
body: You can ask us for a copy of the data we hold about you, have it corrected, or ask us to delete it. Where GDPR or a similar law applies, you can also object to or restrict certain processing, request portability, or complain to your local data protection authority. Email support@localify.dev and we'll respond within a reasonable time.

sections.title: 12. International transfers
body: We and our providers may process data outside your country, including in the United States. Where required, we rely on transfer mechanisms such as adequacy decisions or Standard Contractual Clauses.

sections.title: 13. Children
body: Localify is a developer tool aimed at adults. It isn't intended for children under 16, and we don't knowingly collect personal data from them.

sections.title: 14. Changes to this policy
body: If we change how we handle data, we'll update this page and change the date at the top. If the change is significant, we'll flag it on the website.
